title: User Flows
in30Seconds: A user flow is the sequence of steps a person takes to complete one task with a product, usually the typical or ideal route. Designers draw it as a flow diagram: boxes for screens, arrows for paths, diamonds for decisions, and endpoints where the task ends. Flows expose dead ends and detours before anything is built, but they are plans, not promises, because real users wander.
whyItMatters: People judge a product one task at a time, and a task rarely lives on a single screen. A user flow shows the whole route for one job, finding a book, paying a bill, or booking a seat, so the team can see where people would get stuck before a single screen is built. Flows reveal the quiet failures: a decision with no way out, a detour that costs three extra steps, a task that ends in silence. They also keep the whole team looking at the same path, from the person who writes the words to the person who builds the screens.
learningObjectives: Define a user flow using the working definition from Nielsen Norman Group.
Distinguish a user flow (one task in one product) from a user journey (the whole experience across channels and time).
Name the parts of a flow diagram: screens, decision points, and endpoints.
Explain why flows expose dead ends and detours before anything is built.
Explain why a flow is a plan rather than a promise, and why entry points and edge cases matter.

collegeVersion.heading: The working definition
collegeVersion.body: Nielsen Norman Group's article "User Journeys vs. User Flows" defines a user flow as a set of interactions that describe the typical or ideal set of steps needed to accomplish a common task performed with a product. Three details in that definition carry the meaning. First, a common task is a specific job with a clear finish: renewing a library book, paying a parking ticket, or booking a gym class, not an open-ended goal like "get healthier." Second, the task happens with one product, a single app or website, rather than across a store, a phone call, and an email. Third, the flow describes the typical or ideal route, the path the team hopes the task will take. NN/g notes that flow goals are granular and can usually be accomplished in minutes or hours at most, with a relatively limited set of interactions. That short, contained shape is what separates a flow from the bigger tools around it.

collegeVersion.heading: One task versus the whole experience
collegeVersion.body: The same NN/g article draws the line between a user flow and a user journey. The journey is the wide view: a whole experience spanning channels and time, with the person's actions, thoughts, and feelings recorded along the way. The flow is the micro view: specific, discrete interactions for one common pathway through a product. Consider a rental service. The whole experience of finding an apartment, touring it, applying, and moving in is a journey that spans the website, a phone call, and a paper lease. Entering the card details on the application fee screen is a flow. Both tools are structured around a user goal and seen from the user's point of view, but the flow captures steps and system responses while the journey also captures emotions. User journeys have their own lesson here; the point for now is scope. A team usually needs both, with flows acting as deep dives into the particular moments the journey passes through.

collegeVersion.heading: The diagram: screens, decisions, endpoints
collegeVersion.body: A flow diagram is a drawing of boxes and arrows, and it can be described in words with no design tools at all. Each screen is a box: the borrowed-books list, the renewal button, the confirmation page. Arrows connect the boxes and show the order of the path. A decision point is a diamond, where the path splits depending on what the person chooses or what the system finds, such as "does another patron have a hold on this book?" An endpoint is the rounded shape where the flow finishes, either with success, "renewal confirmed," or with failure, "renewal not available." The Interaction Design Foundation describes the standard symbols: ovals for start and end points, rectangles for steps, and diamonds for decisions. NN/g lists flow charts and task diagrams as common artifacts, and wireflows, which combine flowchart paths with screen layouts. Wireframes themselves belong to a sibling topic; here the diagram is just boxes, arrows, and labels. A flow diagram deliberately leaves feelings out, showing only what happens and what the product does in return.

collegeVersion.heading: Why flows matter, and why they stay plans
collegeVersion.body: Flows earn their keep before anything is built. The Interaction Design Foundation notes that a flow diagram clarifies the sequence of screens a user will move through and lets the team spot potential roadblocks before they become real problems. Consider a meal delivery app whose flow reads: choose meal, check out, pay, order confirmed. Drawn on paper, that flow exposes a dead end: if the payment fails, there is no branch that offers another card, so the task ends in silence. The team fixes the dead end before writing a line of code. The happy path is that smooth, ideal route, and the edge cases are the exceptions around it: an expired card at payment, an empty cart at checkout, a restaurant that closes mid-order. A task also starts from many places. IxDF advises listing the possible entry points, such as direct traffic, organic search, and social media, and a due-date notification, a search result, or an email link can each begin the renewal task, so a flow may need several starting boxes. Finally, a flow is a plan, not a promise. It describes how the team hopes the task will go, and real people skip steps, misread labels, and wander in from unexpected places. NN/g points to usability testing as the strongest way to check whether the mapped steps match how people actually behave; testing methods are a sibling topic.

vocabulary.definition: The sequence of steps a person takes to complete one task with a product, usually the typical or ideal route.
A drawing that maps a user flow with boxes and arrows, showing screens, decision points, and endpoints.
One page or view in a product where the person reads information, makes a choice, or enters details.
A moment in a flow where the path splits based on what the person chooses or what the system finds.
The place where a flow ends, such as a confirmation screen for success or an error screen for failure.
The smooth, ideal route through a task where everything works the first time and no exceptions occur.
An uncommon situation that interrupts the happy path, such as an expired card or a held book.
Any place where a person can start a task, such as a notification, a search result, an ad, or a bookmark.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A user flow is the list of steps one person takes to finish one job in an app or website, like renewing a library book or paying for a parking spot. A flow diagram draws that list as pictures: a box for each screen, an arrow from one box to the next, a diamond where the path splits, and a rounded shape where the job ends. Teams draw the flow before they build anything, because it shows the traps: a step with no way out, a detour that wastes three taps, a finish line nobody reaches. The happy path is the smooth route with no trouble, and edge cases are the exceptions, like a card that expires right at payment.
eli10.analogy: Think of a flow diagram as a recipe card for one dish. It lists the steps in order, from gathering the ingredients to serving the meal, and the cook follows the card from start to finish.
eli10.analogyLimits: The recipe assumes the cook starts at step one with every ingredient in the cupboard. Real users start mid-task, skip steps, substitute ingredients, and wander in from the pantry door, so a flow is a plan to test, not a promise about what people will do.

workedExample: A city library app's team wants to improve renewals. They draw the flow for renewing the borrowed book "The Hidden Tide": the task starts from a due-date notification, a search result, or the Borrowed tab; the person opens the book's record, taps Renew, and the system checks whether another patron has placed a hold. No hold means the renewed confirmation appears, the success endpoint; a hold means a not-renewable screen with the return date, the failure endpoint. The diagram exposes a detour: people arriving from the notification land on the book's record, where the Renew button sits below the fold, forcing a scroll no one expected. The team adds a renewal shortcut to the notification screen, a fix that cost nothing to test because the flow showed the problem first.
commonMistakes: Drawing only the happy path and calling it the flow. Mark the decision points and the failure endpoints too, or the dead ends stay invisible.
Starting every flow at the home screen. Tasks begin from notifications, search results, ads, and links, so trace the real entry points.
Making the diagram so detailed that nobody can read it. A flow is for discussion, so keep to screens, decisions, and endpoints.
Treating the flow as a promise about what users will do. It is a plan; users will wander, so plan to check it with usability testing.

compareContrast.distinction: A flow is the steps for one task in one product; a journey is the whole experience across channels and time, including feelings.
The happy path is the ideal, error-free route; an edge case is an exception that interrupts it, like an expired card at payment.
A screen is a place where the person acts; a decision point is where the path splits because of that act or a system check.

keyTakeaway: A user flow is the sequence of steps for one task in one product, drawn as a diagram of screens, decisions, and endpoints. It exposes dead ends and detours before anything is built, but it stays a plan: entry points vary, edge cases happen, and only testing with real users shows whether the path holds.

options: The set of steps that describe the typical or ideal route a person takes to complete one task with a product
A record of how a person feels across a full week of using a service
A list of every screen a product contains, in no particular order
A study of how competitors price their products
questionBank.explanation: Nielsen Norman Group defines a user flow as a set of interactions describing the typical or ideal steps for a common task with a product. Feelings across a week belong to a journey map, and screen lists or pricing studies are different tools entirely.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the working definition of a user flow

questionBank.prompt: A team is deciding between a user flow and a journey map for a rental app. Which question best settles the choice?
options: How many designers work on the team?
Which font the app uses for headings?
Can the goal be finished in minutes or hours inside one product, or does it stretch across channels and days?
How much the app costs to run each month?
questionBank.explanation: NN/g distinguishes the two by scope: flows suit short, single-product tasks, while journeys suit goals that span channels and time. Team size, typography, and server costs say nothing about that distinction.
questionBank.skill: Applying the flow-versus-journey distinction to a new situation

questionBank.prompt: A flow diagram for booking a table shows a rounded shape labeled 'Start', boxes for each screen, and a diamond labeled 'Table available?'. In the language of flow diagrams, what do the diamond and the shape labeled 'Reservation confirmed' stand for?
options: Two screens the person never sees
A loading delay and a retry button
A menu and a settings panel
A decision point and an endpoint
questionBank.explanation: Diamonds mark decision points, where the path splits on a choice or a system check, and rounded shapes mark endpoints, where the flow finishes. The other options name things flow diagrams do not use.
questionBank.skill: Identifying decision points and endpoints in a flow diagram

questionBank.prompt: A meal delivery app's flow reads: choose meal, check out, pay, order confirmed. Which situation is an edge case the team should plan for?
options: The home screen showing a weekend discount banner
The payment being declined because the card expired
The user changing the app's language setting
The menu sorting items by price
questionBank.explanation: An edge case is an exception that interrupts the happy path, and an expired card at payment is exactly that. Banners, language settings, and sorting are separate features, not exceptions on this route.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing an edge case against a happy path

questionBank.prompt: A library app's renewal flow is drawn starting from the 'Borrowed' tab. Why is it wise to draw the same flow with several starting points?
options: Because people reach the task from many places, such as a due-date notification, a search result, or an email link
Because designers are expected to fill the page with boxes
Because every flow must begin on the home screen
Because the number of starting points is set by the marketing budget
questionBank.explanation: Entry points vary: notifications, search results, links, and ads can all begin a task, and IxDF lists direct traffic, organic search, and social media among them. Starting every flow at the home screen hides how people actually arrive.
questionBank.skill: Explaining why entry points require multiple flow starts

provenance.rightsStatus: reference-only NN/g and IxDF sources; no source prose adapted; all lesson prose and examples original
provenance.transformation: Working definition, macro/micro distinction, artifacts, and the usability-testing link synthesized from NN/g's 'User Journeys vs. User Flows' (Kaplan, 2023); diagram-symbol conventions and entry-point guidance from IxDF's User Flows topic page; flowchart and wireflow framing from NN/g's 'Wireflows' (Laubheimer, 2016). Flow-versus-journey scope references the user-journeys sibling topic only. All examples (library renewal, meal delivery, table booking) are original and invented; no product is named or judged.
